title: What’s New on the Sonoma County Dining Scene This Fall
summary:
Popular Sebastopol cafe opening second location, Montgomery Village gets new restaurant and the Sonoma Spice Queen brings her blends to Santa Rosa.

The post What’s New on the Sonoma County Dining Scene This Fall appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
From a new spice shop to tapas and Mediterranean, Sonoma County’s dining scene is adding new reasons to eat out this fall.

Wild Poppy at The Barlow

Wild Poppy, the west Sebastopol cafe known for breakfast, brunch and lunch, is expanding with a second location in the former Woodfour Brewing space at The Barlow in late September.

The new location will offer grab-and-go meals as well as daytime and evening menus, which are still being developed. Chef-owner Martin Maigaard also hopes to open a tofu factory in the former brewery space next year.

Maigaard, formerly of the now-closed Gypsy Cafe, opened the original Wild Poppy in 2024 with his wife, Danielle.

6780 McKinley St., Suite 160, Sebastopol; 9890 Bodega Highway, Sebastopol. 707-503-6332, thewildpoppycafe.com

Olives and Agave

Tapas and Mediterranean dishes inspired by Spanish and Middle Eastern cuisines are on the menu at this new Montgomery Village restaurant, which opened last week.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by Maza and Tapas (@olivesandagave)

The restaurant is currently open for dinner, with lunch service coming soon. The menu focuses on hot and cold meze, including hummus, baba ghanoush, labneh and tzatziki, along with spanakopita, falafel, fried kibbeh and empanadas. Larger plates include lamb shank tagine, kebabs, whole branzino and half a rotisserie chicken.

The restaurant occupies the former Cascabel space.

909 Village Court, Santa Rosa. 707-843-7365, olivesandagave.com

Sonoma Spice Queen

Wind McAlister, known as the Sonoma Spice Queen, is bringing her spice blends back to Santa Rosa with a new downtown shop.

And this time, it’s got local mojo.

McAlister opened the second location in early September at 404 Mendocino Ave., bringing her organic spice blends, rubs, chiles, peppercorns, salts and sugars north from Petaluma. The shop fills the void left by the departures of Penzeys and Savory Spice.

McAlister has been grinding whole spices and herbs by hand for more than 13 years. In 2013, she was among the first in Sonoma County to obtain a Cottage Food Operator Permit, which allows certain nonperishable foods to be produced in a home kitchen. She now works out of a commercial kitchen.

Her best-selling blend is also her most labor-intensive: vadouvan French curry, a complex mixture of nearly a dozen ingredients, including turmeric, ginger, coriander, garlic and curry leaves.

Her other blends draw from around the world, including Middle Eastern za’atar, Ethiopian berbere and Lebanese sabah baharat. She now offers more than 50 single spices, including saffron, paprika and cinnamon, along with dozens of housemade blends and rubs. Each is ground, mixed, packaged and labeled by hand.

404 Mendocino Ave., Suite D, Santa Rosa; 9 Fourth St., Petaluma. 707-776-7678, sonomaspicequeen.com

title: Historic Petaluma Farmhouse Filled With Charm and Potential
summary:
Built in 1890, this charming Petaluma property includes multiple outbuildings — perfect for a working hobby farm or rustic entertainment spaces.

The post Historic Petaluma Farmhouse Filled With Charm and Potential appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
An 1890s farmhouse on 4.2 acres in Petaluma is currently listed for sale. The two-bedroom, one-bathroom home with multiple outbuildings is priced at $1,299,000. 

Vaulted ceilings give an airiness beyond the home’s 900 square feet. Historic charm remains in wood-plank floors, lemon-yellow lap siding and double-hung windows.

With refurbishment, the property’s weathered outbuildings offer opportunities to create a working hobby farm or studio and entertainment spaces. The property is also zoned R4, which allows for higher-density development.

title: Saddle up at New Country-Western Spur Saloon in Windsor
summary:
Spur Saloon brings saddle seats, batwing doors, cocktails, small plates and a full-on Western vibe to downtown Windsor.

The post Saddle up at New Country-Western Spur Saloon in Windsor appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
You can stomp, step, grapevine and yeehaw all you like at Windsor’s Spur Saloon. A little 10-gallon tomfoolery is welcome, too.

But bronco-busting on the custom-made leather saddle seats will earn you some side-eye. Owner Eric Foster has already bolted those things to the floor twice, and they’re getting loose again.

Spur is Sonoma County’s newest — and pretty much only — Western saloon, cowboy bar and chuckwagon. It’s the antler-chandeliered, “Yellowstone”-set hangout we didn’t know we needed and the occasional dance hall we absolutely did.

Push through the batwing doors, and all that’s missing is a spittoon in the corner and the saloon piano going suddenly quiet.

Never mind. There is a spittoon. You just have to look around for it.

Country, Sonoma-style

Foster and his wife, Christina Keeney, opened the bar and restaurant in August, filling what they saw as a gap in Windsor nightlife — or lack thereof.

They wanted a social place built around food, drinks, dancing and music, where families could grab a meal, friends could grab a drink and locals could cut a rug past 9 p.m. in the sleepy suburb.

As owners of nearby Grata Italian Eatery, which opened in 2020, they had watched Windsor evolve. The empty brewery and tasting room at 9000 Windsor Road, just across from the SMART station, seemed like a missed opportunity.

For several years, Foster and his team kicked around concepts before landing on a country-Western saloon.

“That seemed perfect for the space,” he said.

So far, the response has been gratifyingly neighborly.

“People keep saying, ‘This is what we needed,’ and we wanted to create a place where we would want to go,” Foster said. “But the main drive is a place in town that gets people out and having fun.”

If the restaurant’s Instagram feed is any indication, that’s happening.

The space

Foster and Keeney leaned enthusiastically into the decor, collecting it piece by piece as the project came together.

Saddles were donated or bought online, then mounted on table bases bolted to the floor. Rifle chandeliers and other Western pieces came from a Sacramento country bar that was selling off its decor. Foster spent plenty of time trolling Facebook Marketplace for anything that might fit.

A trip to Jackson Hole provided more inspiration, along with the polished modern-country aesthetic popularized by shows like “Yellowstone.”

“We had a vision in our head,” Foster said.

Foster is clear that Spur is still a work in progress, adapting in real time to how the community wants to use it.

Is it a bar, a restaurant, a third space?

All of the above, he said, though the bar seems to be winning out of the gate.

Cocktails and cold beer have made the horseshoe-shaped bar a destination from its 4 p.m. opening until closing. Knowing it could get busy, the team designed the cocktail program for speed, with several drinks on draft.

Signature cocktails ($15) include the Reverse Cowgirl, with makrut aperitif, gin, mango and mint; Dutton Ranch Water, with yerba mate tequila, lime juice and club soda; and Let’s Go Girls, with blood orange-mandarin vodka, passion fruit, orgeat and lemon. Classic cocktails, beer, wine and mocktails are also available.

But it’s worth wandering farther in.

A long banquette beneath a longhorn-steer mural is prime real estate for kicking back with a few snacks and watching the room — or the televisions.

The separate dining room has high-tops, a cozy lounge area and enough Western bric-a-brac to keep you occupied while you wait for a drink. Dark damask wallpaper gives the room a bordello-meets-Old West-saloon vibe that somehow works.

Bartenders and servers have clearly embraced the assignment, too, going full tilt on Daisy Dukes and boots.

During interviews, Foster said, candidates frequently asked about the dress code.

His answer was essentially: Have fun with it.

They have.

The food

The menu focuses on big flavors and small, shareable plates, with bison sliders, smoked brisket tamales, buffalo chicken dip, jalapeño-pepper egg rolls and ceviche among the early favorites.

The limited all-electric kitchen helped shape the menu, forcing Foster to get creative with just an oven, smoker and a few induction burners.

Dips, ceviches, salads, chili and a small selection of barbecue make for a fun assortment — and some very good bites.

Eventually, Foster envisions a dependable core menu of small plates supplemented by nightly smoker specials, such as tri-tip or ribs.

For now, think smorgasbord rather than four-course meal.

Best bets

Smoked Onion Dip, $13: Just what it says: a big old bowl of onion dip with a hint of smoke and straight-up chips. Add caviar if you’ve just struck oil. It’s pricey but tasty.

Ahi Ceviche Tostada, $20: Solid, simple and fresh, with ruby-red tuna, chipotle aioli, pickled onion and radish. Pepitas and fresh avocado class it up.

Elote Salad, $15: Sweet corn with tangy lime dressing, salty cotija cheese and a few grinds of pepper.

Bison Sliders, $19: One of the best things on the menu. Juicy mini burgers slathered with chimichurri and red-eye glaze. Two-bite brilliance.

Loaded Baked Potato, $19: I’m a sucker for a baked potato. Cover it with cheese béchamel and candied bacon and I’m a goner. Nostalgic and perfect.

Frito Pie, $12: A love-it-or-hate-it proposition. Chili, cheese, tomatoes and Fritos will always have a place in my heart.

More details

For an upcoming Dolly Parton tribute on Sept. 25, Spur will feature musician Max Vogel, along with a Dolly Parton look-alike contest.

Live music is planned about twice a month, with more on the way, along with line dancing, music bingo, karaoke brunch and happy hour.

Spur is family-friendly before 9 p.m., when it becomes 21 and over.

You can show up in boots and a cowboy hat, or just show up. Either way, you’ll probably end up yeehawing at least once.

Open 4-11 p.m. Sunday through Thursday and 4 p.m. to midnight Friday and Saturday. 9000 Windsor Road, Windsor, 707-620-0193, instagram.com/spur.saloon.windsor

title: Modern Home in Bucolic East Napa Hits the Market
summary:
Remodeled by an award-winning Mill Valley architecture firm, the agrarian-style Napa home includes a massive fruit orchard, outdoor pizza ovens and a pickleball court.

The post Modern Home in Bucolic East Napa Hits the Market appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
The reimagined home of early-computing tech entrepreneur and WillaKenzie Estate winery founder Bernard Lacroute and his wife Ronni is currently listed for sale. The 7,926-square-foot estate on 10.77 acres in Napa is seeking $16,950,000.

The 6,725-square-foot, four-bedroom main home and a 1,200-square-foot, two-bedroom guesthouse — remodeled with a striking modernity by Mill Valley-based Sutton Suzuki Architects — are surrounded by trees and meandering paths.

A 1.3-acre lily pond runs the length of the two dwellings. The property’s 90 olive trees produce estate olive oil, and a 98-tree fruit orchard includes 35 citrus trees. There’s a rose garden and raised beds for vegetables and cutting flowers.

A full outdoor kitchen with two pizza ovens sets the stage for farm-to-table living. A pool with integrated spa, a bocce court, and a tennis and pickleball court offer recreation amid the bucolic setting. 

The home’s expansive walls of glass connect to the natural surroundings, while high ceilings give interiors light and a sense of grandeur. The style is angular and restrained, with areas of vertical wood cladding inside and outside.

Agrarian style is brought inside via rustic beams that repeat, or are arranged in grids, along the ceilings. A variety of glass, clean-lined light fixtures provide a modern yet graceful finish.

For more information on this home at 3027 Vichy Ave. in Napa, contact listing agent Hillary Ryan, 707-312-2105, 707-224-8000; Sotheby’s International Realty – St. Helena Brokerage, 1229 Adams St., St. Helena, sothebysrealty.com/eng/sales/detail/180-l-86828-wn98mm/3027-vichy-avenue-napa-ca-94558

title: 90 Kinds of Instant Ramen? Meet Graton Resort’s Wildly Fun New Neon Kitty
summary:
Nearly 90 kinds of instant ramen, Korean hot dogs, onigiri and viral Asian snacks fill the shelves at Graton Resort & Casino’s colorful new Neon Kitty.

The post 90 Kinds of Instant Ramen? Meet Graton Resort’s Wildly Fun New Neon Kitty appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Chef Jennifer Murphy-Ellamar was, understandably, feeling a little thirsty after taste-testing nearly 90 varieties of instant ramen for the shelves of Neon Kitty, the new market and noodlery at Graton Resort & Casino.

Standing before a wall of crinkly plastic packages and cardboard bowls she had handpicked from across Asia, she was searching for a particular favorite: Menraku Tonkotsu, with its creamy pork broth and chewy noodles.

“This is really good,” she said, pulling a package from the shelves she calls her ramen library.

With K-pop humming in the background and a dozen golden maneki-neko waving their lucky paws at us, the choice between creamy tonkotsu and something coated in screaming-hot chiles wasn’t difficult. Screaming-hot chiles never work out in my favor.

So why was a fine-dining chef more accustomed to caviar, lobster and Wagyu tasting menus spending her days with a plastic soup spoon and getting salty tonkotsu broth facials?

Adding “ramen sommelier” to her résumé was simply too irresistible to pass up. And someone had to write the tasting notes for the staff.

All-night noodle party

“A restaurant offering instant ramen is crazy,” Murphy-Ellamar said. “I never thought I’d be doing something like this in my career.”

On opening day, she bustled around what she describes as an “Asian bodega” inside the casino. Flanked by two giant lucky cats, pink neon signs and enough cartoon animals to overcrowd a manga convention, it’s a tween dream wrapped in a fuzzy blanket of kawaii.

Trying to describe Neon Kitty as a cafe, convenience store, bodega or snack bar doesn’t quite do it justice. It’s simply Neon Kitty, and somehow that makes perfect sense.

It is also an oddly obvious solution to a problem at the 13-year-old casino: how to feed guests late at night.

With a hotel, multiple clubs and entertainment venues, in addition to gaming floors, requiring food service around the clock, Murphy-Ellamar turned to one of her favorite foods for something that could be served at any hour — fast, hot and inexpensive, without requiring a full restaurant meal.

Whether it’s 4 p.m. or 4 a.m., the process is simple: Pick a ramen. Any ramen.

Staff members can point out the options — spicy or mild, beef or pork, and everything in between — if you’re stumped. Take the package to the counter and watch as a high-tech machine cooks the noodles at precisely the right temperature. Add fresh toppings like pork, corn, nori and bamboo shoots, and within minutes you’re hunched over a steaming bowl of noodles.

If you’ve experienced the delightfully lowbrow appeal of instant ramen, whether out of economic necessity or pure laziness, the attraction is easy to understand.

“Every culture has their own instant noodle,” Murphy-Ellamar said. “Each one has a different texture. Some are salty and spicy, some are more subtle, and you can really geek out on it.”

The dried-noodle selection includes Vietnamese pho, Thai curries, Chinese seafood broths and dozens of other variations.

But ramen is only part of Neon Kitty.

Viral vibes

Murphy-Ellamar spent months not only handpicking noodles but also creating a lineup of grab-and-go foods made in-house: Japanese egg salad sandwiches, steamed bao and Korean hot dogs, along with social-media darlings like Vietnamese chè thái, a fruit dessert, and Taiwanese fan tuan, a sticky rice breakfast roll.

There are also onigiri, Spam musubi, dumplings, rice bowls, candies, milk tea drinks and shelves of brightly packaged snacks.

The inspiration clearly comes from Japanese convenience stores, known as konbini, which are beloved well beyond Japan for their surprisingly good prepared foods. But Neon Kitty casts a much wider net, drawing from China, Korea, Japan, the Philippines, Vietnam, Thailand and Indonesia.

“It’s not fusion,” Murphy-Ellamar said. “It’s respecting each individual culture.”

Nostalgia or discovery

For a wide swath of Graton’s customers, Neon Kitty offers a familiar taste of home.

The resort draws a significant Asian clientele and regularly hosts Asian performers. A treat that sends one customer into a TikTok-fueled squeal — hint: #chèthái is trending — may be an everyday favorite for someone else.

“A lot of this is nostalgia for me,” Murphy-Ellamar said.

Growing up, the Vietnamese food her mother packed for school sometimes drew teasing from classmates. Decades later, many of those same flavors have become social-media stars.

And that’s exactly the point.

While I’m pondering whether the butter-flavored potato chips are a good idea — yes, yes, they are — someone else might be getting warm fuzzies over a whipped-cream-and-strawberry sandwich reminiscent of a childhood lunch box.

Also a great call.

The changing face of Graton

Neon Kitty is one of several new restaurants reshaping the food lineup at the Rohnert Park casino under Murphy-Ellamar and her husband, chef Roy Ellamar.

Over the past two years, the couple has developed AYA, the resort’s new fine-dining restaurant, along with SoCo Dough Co. and Playbook sports bar. Neon Kitty, in the casino’s new nonsmoking wing, is the latest addition, with more projects still in the works.

But while Neon Kitty is about as far from white-tablecloth dining as you can get, Murphy-Ellamar is clear that it isn’t a throwaway. The same obsessive attention applies here, redirected toward fast-casual craveability and fun.

“It’s impossible to walk by this restaurant and not want to come in,” she said.

And if you decide to taste your way through all 90 ramen varieties, grab a fizzy Ramune soda, milk tea or melon juice.

You’ll need it.

288 Golf Course Drive W., Rohnert Park, 707-588-7100, graton.com/fast-casual/neon-kitty

title: Where to Get the Best Pancakes in Sonoma County
summary:
From fluffy buttermilk to lemon ricotta, here are some of our favorite pancakes in Sonoma County to enjoy on National Pancake Day.

The post Where to Get the Best Pancakes in Sonoma County appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
From ancient Rome to millennial brunch culture, pancakes have long been a breakfast staple — and a natural companion to a mimosa.

Across Sonoma County, chefs put their own spin on the classic stack. Here are some favorites, from fluffy buttermilk pancakes to thin Swedish-style versions and a Dutch Baby big enough to share. Enjoy them on National Pancake Day, Sept. 26, or any day of the year.

Best Newcomer

Dolce Rosa: These plate-size ricotta pancakes are good enough on their own, but the espresso-spiked mascarpone and chocolate syrup, finished with a dusting of cocoa, push them firmly into dessert territory. Breakfast, meet tiramisu. 4910 Sonoma Highway, Suite B, Santa Rosa. 707-931-4625, instagram.com/dolcerosacafe

The Classic

Dierk’s Parkside Café: Simple, fluffy pancakes come with eggs and bacon at this longtime Santa Rosa breakfast favorite. 404 Santa Rosa Ave., Santa Rosa, 707-573-5955, dierksparkside.com

Sweetest Treat

Cafe Carrusel: Strawberry Heaven pink pancakes with sweet glaze and colorful marshmallows are a childhood dream at this pink-on-pink bruncheria in downtown Santa Rosa. The morning-centric menu also includes matcha, ube, blueberry, red velvet, Oreo and classic buttermilk pancakes. 630 Third St., Santa Rosa, 707-655-8365, instagram.com/cafe_carrusel

Sleeper Hit

Fandee’s Restaurant: Rich, fluffy lemon-ricotta pancakes are served with berries and vanilla crème anglaise. 7824 Covert Lane, Sebastopol, 707-829-2462, fandeesrestaurant.com

Best Lemon-Ricotta Hotcake

Acorn Cafe: At the former Oakville Grocery site, Acorn Cafe serves a lemon-ricotta hotcake with house lemon curd, whipped ricotta and oat crumble, topped with lemon-lavender ice cream. 124 Matheson St., Healdsburg, 707-955-7001, acornhealdsburg.com

Big and Buttery

Jeffrey’s Hillside Cafe: Buttermilk pancakes arrive as large as dinner plates, accompanied by two eggs and a choice of bacon, sausage or ham. 2901 Fourth St., Santa Rosa, 707-546-6317, jeffreyshillsidecafe.com

Brunch Favorite

Verano Cafe: Plate-size lemon pancakes get their distinctive texture from cottage cheese, eggs and lemon. Pair them with a mimosa — passion fruit is a favorite — or a cup of coffee. 18976 Sonoma Highway, Sonoma, 707-931-6837, veranocafesonoma.com

Bavarian-Style

Brother’s Cafe: The owners of Sebastopol’s Hole in the Wall opened this sister restaurant in 2022. The standout is the Dutch Baby, a German-style pancake with caramelized sugar and apples. 3135 Cleveland Ave., Santa Rosa, 707-541-6345, brotherscafesr.com

Swedish-Style

Thin, crepe-like pancakes from Sweden aren’t hard to find in Sonoma County.

Baked on the River: The Pancakes from the North are thin and folded, served with vanilla whipped cream, lingonberry jam, butter and maple syrup. 16390 Fourth St., Guerneville, 707-865-6060, bakedontheriver.com

Stockhome: These plate-sized pancakes have crisp edges and a hint of sweetness, and come with vanilla whipped cream and berries. 220 Western Ave., Petaluma, 707-981-8511, stockhomepetaluma.com

Fill ’Er Up

Sax’s Joint: For sheer size, it’s hard to beat the restaurant’s enormous pancake, which is roughly the size of a pizza and made with a half-gallon of batter. 317 Petaluma Blvd. S., Petaluma, 707-559-3021, saxsjoint.com

Farm-to-Table

Americana: Pancakes, hot off the griddle, are top-notch. Choose from classic, blueberry or chocolate-chip pancakes, served with housemade vanilla-cider maple syrup, whipped cream and seasonal fruit. 162 N. Main St., Sebastopol, 707-827-3309; 205 Fifth St., Suite A, Santa Rosa, 707-755-1548, americanasonomacounty.com

Best with Your Dog

Howard Station Cafe: This dog-friendly, locomotive-themed cafe serves stacks of buttermilk, blueberry and banana-walnut pancakes. 3611 Bohemian Highway, Occidental, 707-874-2838, howardstationcafe.com, instagram.com/howardstationcafe

Maci Martell contributed to this article.

title: At Chateau Montelena, Napa Valley’s Past Comes to Life
summary:
A historic Calistoga winery pairs classic wines and a storied estate with an AI-assisted look at the people and places that shaped its past.

The post At Chateau Montelena, Napa Valley’s Past Comes to Life appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
In the last couple of years, Napa Valley has seen a wave of dramatic winery makeovers, from Robert Mondavi Winery’s multimillion-dollar renovation to Beaulieu Vineyard’s recently unveiled refresh. As impressive as those transformations can be, there is something appealing about stepping back in time to the region’s early days.

At Chateau Montelena in Calistoga, classic Napa Valley wines are poured inside a Gothic-style stone castle built in the late 19th century. Now, in a nod to the modern era, visitors can explore the winery’s 144-year history through a storytelling experience that brings historical photographs to life with artificial intelligence.

The story

In 1882, A.L. Tubbs, a San Francisco entrepreneur who had made his fortune during the Gold Rush, bought 254 acres at the foot of Mount St. Helena with plans to build a winery. He planted vineyards on the property, and by 1896, A.L. Tubbs Winery was among Napa Valley’s largest.

The winery closed during Prohibition. Tubbs’s grandson later revived the operation, but it shut down again and the vineyards were sold in 1945.

In 1958, Yort Wing Frank and his wife, Jeanie, bought the property and made the winery their home. To evoke the couple’s homeland in China, Yort created Jade Lake, a water garden with bridges, pagodas and willow trees.

Lee and Helen Paschich acquired the estate and winery a decade later, laying the groundwork for a return to commercial wine production. In 1972, Lee sold the majority of the property to Jim Barrett, a successful business lawyer who dreamed of starting a winery. Barrett replanted the original vineyard with Cabernet Sauvignon.

Four years later, Chateau Montelena’s 1973 Chardonnay made history when it bested its French counterparts in the now-famous 1976 “Judgment of Paris” tasting.

Today, Jim Barrett’s son, Bo, runs the winery. More than 100 acres of the estate are planted to vines, primarily Cabernet Sauvignon, Primitivo and Zinfandel, along with smaller plantings of Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot and Petite Sirah. Last year, the winery added a 72-acre Chardonnay vineyard in Carneros.

The vibe

Before you even reach the ivy-covered winery, the beauty of the estate is hard to miss. From the lower-level parking area, a path leads toward the tasting room through stands of California coast redwoods and a serene water garden, where small islands are linked by bright red bridges. Wine club members can picnic in pagodas on the islands.

Inside, the tasting room has dark wood and exposed stone walls, giving it a distinctly old-world feel. Beyond the entrance bar is a small museum devoted to the winery’s history, followed by another bar and several rooms for private experiences. A front patio welcomes walk-in visitors on weekends.

On the palate

Chateau Montelena’s wines remain true to the restrained style of its early years. Winemaker Matt Crafton makes Chardonnays with a Chablis-like character, while the Cabernet Sauvignons balance power with prominent tannins rather than topple over the top.

The 2023 Napa Valley Chardonnay ($75) is a good reminder of why the variety put the winery on the world wine map. Showing plenty of minerality and acidity, the wine has aromas and flavors of green apples and citrus, and a weighty mouthfeel.

The 2024 Potter Valley Riesling ($45) is a pleasant surprise. Made in an off-dry style, it is floral and bright, with notes of nectarine, Meyer lemon and citrus without seeming overly sweet.

The 2023 Estate Zinfandel ($50), from Calistoga, is the opposite of a jammy fruit bomb. It has a beautiful mixed-berry aroma, with flavors to match, accented by savory, herbaceous notes.

Tastings range from $65 for a selection of current releases to $110 for a vineyard tour and tasting. A private, guided exploration of the vineyards and chateau, including library vintages, costs $300.

Beyond the bottle

If you have seen “Bottle Shock,” the 2008 movie loosely based on the 1976 “Judgment of Paris” tasting, Chateau Montelena’s “Story Behind the Bottle” experience ($75) offers a more grounded way to learn what really happened.

The tasting takes place at an eight-seat bar, where framed historical photographs are animated with artificial intelligence. The effect is a little like the moving portraits in the “Harry Potter” films. A human host provides the narration, telling stories from the winery’s early years while pouring current and library releases.

Chateau Montelena is open from 9:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. daily. 1429 Tubbs Lane, Calistoga. 707-942-5105, montelena.com

Tina Caputo is a wine, food and travel writer whose work has appeared in numerous publications, including SevenFifty Daily, Visit California, HuffPost and Sonoma magazine. Follow Tina on Bluesky @winebroad and view her website at tinacaputo.com.

title: Our Favorite Glamping Spots in Sonoma County
summary:
Become one with nature while enjoying some creature comforts at these luxe glamping spots in Sonoma County.

The post Our Favorite Glamping Spots in Sonoma County appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Sleeping under the stars sounds wonderful until you remember that sleeping on the ground isn’t exactly comfortable and that hot showers are a good thing. In Sonoma County, you can have the best of both worlds — being one with nature while enjoying some creature comforts — at these luxe glamping spots.

Safari West, Santa Rosa

Consistently ranked as one of America’s best glamping spots by USA Today 10Best. Safari through Sonoma’s Serengeti, then spend the night in a luxury tent cabin on the 400-acre wildlife preserve. Overnight stays include a chorus of rare birds as your alarm clock and a continental breakfast. Book a South African-style braai (barbecue) for dinner at the Savannah Café for an additional charge. 3115 Porter Creek Road, Santa Rosa. 800-616-2695, safariwest.com

Sugarloaf Ridge State Park, Kenwood

Four permanent glamping tents are tucked away in the campground at Sugarloaf Ridge State Park in Kenwood. Each canvas tent features a queen bed, futon lounge chairs, rugs, tables, lights, and firewood. Other amenities include a picnic table, fire ring, and outdoor seating, plus 4,900 acres of pristine natural wonder including waterfalls, wildflowers, and majestic redwoods along the miles of hiking and biking trails. The park hosts guided events throughout the year, plus stargazing at the Robert Ferguson observatory. 2605 Adobe Canyon Road, Kenwood. 707-833-5712, sugarloafpark.org

Wildhaven, Healdsburg

Just steps from the Russian River, choose between safari-style canvas tents or cabins equipped with a bed, linens, heated mattress pads, towels, lights, electric outlets and heaters. Each site has a picnic table, fire pit, and access to a communal cooking area with barbecues and sinks. Guests can enjoy easy access to hiking trails, private access to the Russian River for a cooling afternoon dip or float, plus Saturdays bring morning yoga sessions and tasting events with local winemakers. 2411 Alexander Valley Road, Healdsburg. 707-283-7773, wildhavensonoma.com

Lake Sonoma, Geyserville

Camping at Lake Sonoma Recreation Area in Geyserville got an upgrade this summer when The Ranch at Lake Sonoma opened the first of 38 new glamping spots. The luxury canvas tents on wooden platforms are outfitted with full-sized beds and heaters. The second phase of tents will be safari tents from Botswana (which ranch manager Nikki Baxes describes as “showstoppers”) that are expected to be installed by late summer. Guests also have access to hot showers, flushing toilets, barbecues and fire rings, while the Ranch’s barn bar is a short walk away.

Despite the luxury trappings, there’s still plenty of wilderness to be found along the 17,000-acre park’s 50 miles of hiking trails. The highlight of Sonoma County’s newest glamping destination might be the views: sunlight sparkles on the lake by day, and at night, the absence of light pollution makes stargazing spectacular. 100 Lake Sonoma Overlook Road, Geyserville. 707-494-4449, theranchatlakesonoma.com

AutoCamp Russian River, Guerneville

At AutoCamp in Guerneville, guests can choose between staying in a sleek Airstream trailer, luxury tent, or the adorable and budget-friendly Happier Camper, with as much luxury as possible packed into its petite 42 square feet. The clubhouse features spa-style showers and bathrooms, general store, and a complimentary morning granola and coffee bar. On-site bike rentals mean Johnson’s Beach on the Russian River is an easy pedal away. Dog-friendly Airstreams are available for an extra fee. 4120 Old Cazadero Road, Guerneville. 888-405-7553, autocamp.com

River Electric, Guerneville

The Russian River area’s newest resort features 46 furnished tents with hotel-like amenities and access to a central bathhouse. The draw here is the resort’s two sparkling pools: a 60-foot round, family-friendly pool and a smaller adults-only area. The pool bar serves meals until 8 p.m., plus cocktails and snacks until 10 p.m. Stays include a continental breakfast. Although checkout is 11 a.m., guests have until 6 p.m. that day to enjoy the pool and restaurant. The resort also offers day passes to those not staying overnight. 16101 Neeley Road, Guerneville. 707-937-8915, theriverelectric.com

Dawn Ranch, Guerneville

In addition to top-tier dining and luxurious cottages, Dawn Ranch offers nine glamping accommodations near the property’s 120-year-old apple orchard from April to October for those who want a more immersive back-to-nature experience. Queen cabin tents feature private baths, while the king tents have shared bathroom facilities with luxury in mind. At the end of the day enjoy s’mores with guests at the communal campfire or at your accommodation’s private firepit. Borrow one of the resort’s Fender guitars for a sing-along before tucking in for the night. 16467 Highway 116, Guerneville. 707-869-0656, dawnranch.com

Sonoma Zipline Adventures, Occidental

Five treehouses, similar to yurts, form an aerial village in redwood treetops on the Alliance Redwoods property in west county. (There’s also a sixth similar ADA-compliant and accessible ground-level structure.) Every treehouse sleeps up to four, and stays include two zipline tours with Sonoma Zipline Adventures — one on the day you arrive and another before you depart. A gourmet dinner and hot breakfast will also be delivered to your arboreal retreat. 6250 Bohemian Highway, Occidental. 888-494-7868, sonomacanopytours.com

Salmon Creek Ranch, Bodega

Forget the tent. At Salmon Creek Ranch you can stay in a dreamy treehouse complete with heat, electricity and a bathroom. Located on a 400-acre working ranch on the Sonoma Coast, Eagle’s Nest Treehouse is accessed via a 30-foot spiral staircase. It features a queen bed, coffee machine and a wraparound deck for lounging — when you’re not hanging out with the ranch’s resident ducks, cows, goats and livestock guardian dogs. 1400 Bay Hill Road, Bodega. 707-775-9604, salmoncreekranch.com

title: This Spaghetti Squash Recipe Combines the Best of Summer and Fall
summary:
Once you’ve raked a fork through cooked spaghetti squash, there are myriad ways to enjoy the noodles. This recipe is one of our favorites.

The post This Spaghetti Squash Recipe Combines the Best of Summer and Fall appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Not long after pomegranates first appear and we can still find summer produce at our farmers markets, winter squashes reach out to connect late summer with early fall. It is a season of remarkable bounty and deliciousness.

Spaghetti squash, with its sun-like exterior and cooked flesh that shreds into slender noodles, hence its name, is perhaps the best transitional treat. Denser winter squashes require slow and somewhat lengthy cooking, but spaghetti squash can be roasted or steamed relatively quickly and a fork is all you need to extract the noodles. The taste is earthy and slightly sweet, but not as sweet as other winter squashes.

Once you’ve raked a fork through the cooked squash, there are myriad ways to enjoy the noodles, chilled or hot. Thai-inspired salad with spicy dressing makes a refreshing meal on hot days. Make spaghetti squash carbonara, a gluten-free delight without any sacrifice of flavor, or on chilly nights, fry sliced mushrooms and sausages and toss them with the “noodles.” Warm spaghetti squash with five-spice butter makes a delicious bed for roasted chicken.

But in early fall when we still have a colorful cornucopia of cherry tomatoes just begging to be plucked from their stems, combine them with spaghetti squash and tiny shrimp, then toss in a sweet-tart vinaigrette. It makes a dazzling dish to enjoy at home or at a picnic or potluck, as it travels well.

Spaghetti Squash, Cherry Tomatoes and Bay Shrimp with Honey-Pepper Vinaigrette

Serves 4

  • 8 ounces bay shrimp (aka Oregon pink shrimp)
  • 1 small shallot, minced
  • 2 garlic cloves, minced
  • ¾ tsp. kosher salt, plus more to taste
  • 2 tbsp. sherry vinegar
  • 2 tsp. freshly cracked black peppercorns, plus more to taste
  • 2 tbsp. honey, warmed
  • ⅓ to ½ cup extra-virgin olive oil
  • 2 tbsp. shredded fresh spearmint leaves, optional
  • 5 cups (approximately) cooked spaghetti squash, lightly chilled (see note)
  • 1 ½ cups cherry tomatoes, halved if small, quartered if large
  • Spearmint leaves, optional, for garnish

Put the shrimp into a strainer set over a deep bowl or the kitchen sink to drain.

Meanwhile, combine the shallot, garlic and kosher salt in a small bowl, add the vinegar, and set aside for 15 minutes. Stir in the pepper, honey and 1/3 cup of olive oil. Taste and correct for salt, pepper and acid, adding the remaining olive oil if it is too tart. Fold in the mint, if using.

Put the spaghetti squash into a medium bowl, add the cherry tomatoes and half the vinaigrette, and use two forks to toss together gently. Tip into a shallow serving bowl or divide among four individual bowls. Top with the shrimp and spoon the remaining dressing over everything.

Garnish with spearmint leaves, if using, and enjoy right away.

Note: Steaming spaghetti squash instead of roasting in the oven results in the best flavor and light texture ideal for enjoying in these recipes. For about 5 cups, cut a 2 1/2 pound squash in half lengthwise, season lightly with salt, and set both halves, cut side up, in a broad steamer set over a pot of simmering water. Steam until the flesh about half an inch from the peel is just tender when pierced with a fork; do not overcook. Remove it from the heat and let it cool until easy to handle.

Use a grapefruit spoon or a paring knife to remove the seeds and the first thin layer of pulp. Discard it or set seeds aside to roast. Using a dinner fork, work from one end to the other to remove the flesh, which shreds itself as you pull on it. Spread it over a platter or baking sheet to cool completely and then proceed with the recipe.

title: Katie Ambrosi Shares Harvest Season Favorites in Wine Country
summary:
As the new executive director of Wine Road, Katie Ambrosi highlights the joys that have made Wine Country a desired destination for decades.

The post Katie Ambrosi Shares Harvest Season Favorites in Wine Country appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
When Katie Ambrosi took over in June as executive director of Wine Road, an organization that for half a century has helped promote wine tourism in the Russian River, Dry Creek, and Alexander valleys, she stepped into a role that had been held by her predecessor for 25 years during a challenging time for the industry. The Healdsburg native, whose nickname is “Sparkles,” is focused on highlighting the fundamental joys that have made Wine Country a destination for decades.

“Everything’s changed. People are looking at wine in a different way,” she says. “People need to remember that wine tastes good and it’s fun. It’s great with food. It’s something that’s always been a part of celebrations and gatherings and everyday enjoyment. If we can remember that, it goes a long way.”

The mom of two boys — one in college, the other in elementary school — admits to being Healdsburg-centric, but did venture out of the ’burg some when it comes to sharing her favorite things about the harvest season in Sonoma County.

Ambrosi is a keen seamstress and frequently whips up dresses made from thrifted linens, including a gold number she made from a tablecloth for last year’s Sonoma County Harvest Fair celebration. “It showcases so many great things with Sonoma County wine and food all in one spot,” she says of the Harvest Fair. She’s already planning how to bedazzle her dress for the Red, White & Sparkle theme for this year’s Taste, Toast & Celebrate event, on Oct. 10. harvestfair.org

While kids can satisfy their sweet tooth going door-to-door on Halloween, Ambrosi heads to Dry Creek Kitchen for the chocolate peanut butter bar, a grown-up take that puts regular peanut butter cups to shame. “The candy bar dessert is exceptional. You have to make sure you save enough room that you’re able to eat that when you go there.” drycreekkitchen.com

Though not as well known as Geyserville’s famous holiday tractor parade, the town’s annual Fall Colors Festival is a must-do for Ambrosi. “I religiously attend. I have an orange and black full-circle skirt, so I bring my love of vintage dressing to it,” she says, explaining that her costume is tied to the festival’s classic car show. Held on the last Sunday of October, the day also includes a pancake breakfast, a scarecrow display and a pumpkin-decorating contest. visitgeyserville.com/fall-colors

Chances are good you’ll find Ambrosi stepping up to the mic at one of the many local karaoke nights. “I love to sing karaoke, so I have a personal challenge. I want to do one week where we do one song at a different spot every night in Sonoma County.” Two of her favorite haunts are on opposite ends of the county: Railroad Station in Cloverdale and Willowbrook Ale House in Petaluma. railroadstationbarandgrille.com; facebook.com/willowbrook.a.house

50 wineries pouring; local chefs will serve small bites.

title: What’s New on the Sonoma County Dining Scene This Fall
summary:
Popular Sebastopol cafe opening second location, Montgomery Village gets new restaurant and the Sonoma Spice Queen brings her blends to Santa Rosa.

The post What’s New on the Sonoma County Dining Scene This Fall appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
From a new spice shop to tapas and Mediterranean, Sonoma County’s dining scene is adding new reasons to eat out this fall.

Wild Poppy at The Barlow

Wild Poppy, the west Sebastopol cafe known for breakfast, brunch and lunch, is expanding with a second location in the former Woodfour Brewing space at The Barlow in late September.

The new location will offer grab-and-go meals as well as daytime and evening menus, which are still being developed. Chef-owner Martin Maigaard also hopes to open a tofu factory in the former brewery space next year.

Maigaard, formerly of the now-closed Gypsy Cafe, opened the original Wild Poppy in 2024 with his wife, Danielle.

6780 McKinley St., Suite 160, Sebastopol; 9890 Bodega Highway, Sebastopol. 707-503-6332, thewildpoppycafe.com

Olives and Agave

Tapas and Mediterranean dishes inspired by Spanish and Middle Eastern cuisines are on the menu at this new Montgomery Village restaurant, which opened last week.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by Maza and Tapas (@olivesandagave)

The restaurant is currently open for dinner, with lunch service coming soon. The menu focuses on hot and cold meze, including hummus, baba ghanoush, labneh and tzatziki, along with spanakopita, falafel, fried kibbeh and empanadas. Larger plates include lamb shank tagine, kebabs, whole branzino and half a rotisserie chicken.

The restaurant occupies the former Cascabel space.

909 Village Court, Santa Rosa. 707-843-7365, olivesandagave.com

Sonoma Spice Queen

Wind McAlister, known as the Sonoma Spice Queen, is bringing her spice blends back to Santa Rosa with a new downtown shop.

And this time, it’s got local mojo.

McAlister opened the second location in early September at 404 Mendocino Ave., bringing her organic spice blends, rubs, chiles, peppercorns, salts and sugars north from Petaluma. The shop fills the void left by the departures of Penzeys and Savory Spice.

McAlister has been grinding whole spices and herbs by hand for more than 13 years. In 2013, she was among the first in Sonoma County to obtain a Cottage Food Operator Permit, which allows certain nonperishable foods to be produced in a home kitchen. She now works out of a commercial kitchen.

Her best-selling blend is also her most labor-intensive: vadouvan French curry, a complex mixture of nearly a dozen ingredients, including turmeric, ginger, coriander, garlic and curry leaves.

Her other blends draw from around the world, including Middle Eastern za’atar, Ethiopian berbere and Lebanese sabah baharat. She now offers more than 50 single spices, including saffron, paprika and cinnamon, along with dozens of housemade blends and rubs. Each is ground, mixed, packaged and labeled by hand.

404 Mendocino Ave., Suite D, Santa Rosa; 9 Fourth St., Petaluma. 707-776-7678, sonomaspicequeen.com

title: Saddle up at New Country-Western Spur Saloon in Windsor
summary:
Spur Saloon brings saddle seats, batwing doors, cocktails, small plates and a full-on Western vibe to downtown Windsor.

The post Saddle up at New Country-Western Spur Saloon in Windsor appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
You can stomp, step, grapevine and yeehaw all you like at Windsor’s Spur Saloon. A little 10-gallon tomfoolery is welcome, too.

But bronco-busting on the custom-made leather saddle seats will earn you some side-eye. Owner Eric Foster has already bolted those things to the floor twice, and they’re getting loose again.

Spur is Sonoma County’s newest — and pretty much only — Western saloon, cowboy bar and chuckwagon. It’s the antler-chandeliered, “Yellowstone”-set hangout we didn’t know we needed and the occasional dance hall we absolutely did.

Push through the batwing doors, and all that’s missing is a spittoon in the corner and the saloon piano going suddenly quiet.

Never mind. There is a spittoon. You just have to look around for it.

Country, Sonoma-style

Foster and his wife, Christina Keeney, opened the bar and restaurant in August, filling what they saw as a gap in Windsor nightlife — or lack thereof.

They wanted a social place built around food, drinks, dancing and music, where families could grab a meal, friends could grab a drink and locals could cut a rug past 9 p.m. in the sleepy suburb.

As owners of nearby Grata Italian Eatery, which opened in 2020, they had watched Windsor evolve. The empty brewery and tasting room at 9000 Windsor Road, just across from the SMART station, seemed like a missed opportunity.

For several years, Foster and his team kicked around concepts before landing on a country-Western saloon.

“That seemed perfect for the space,” he said.

So far, the response has been gratifyingly neighborly.

“People keep saying, ‘This is what we needed,’ and we wanted to create a place where we would want to go,” Foster said. “But the main drive is a place in town that gets people out and having fun.”

If the restaurant’s Instagram feed is any indication, that’s happening.

The space

Foster and Keeney leaned enthusiastically into the decor, collecting it piece by piece as the project came together.

Saddles were donated or bought online, then mounted on table bases bolted to the floor. Rifle chandeliers and other Western pieces came from a Sacramento country bar that was selling off its decor. Foster spent plenty of time trolling Facebook Marketplace for anything that might fit.

A trip to Jackson Hole provided more inspiration, along with the polished modern-country aesthetic popularized by shows like “Yellowstone.”

“We had a vision in our head,” Foster said.

Foster is clear that Spur is still a work in progress, adapting in real time to how the community wants to use it.

Is it a bar, a restaurant, a third space?

All of the above, he said, though the bar seems to be winning out of the gate.

Cocktails and cold beer have made the horseshoe-shaped bar a destination from its 4 p.m. opening until closing. Knowing it could get busy, the team designed the cocktail program for speed, with several drinks on draft.

Signature cocktails ($15) include the Reverse Cowgirl, with makrut aperitif, gin, mango and mint; Dutton Ranch Water, with yerba mate tequila, lime juice and club soda; and Let’s Go Girls, with blood orange-mandarin vodka, passion fruit, orgeat and lemon. Classic cocktails, beer, wine and mocktails are also available.

But it’s worth wandering farther in.

A long banquette beneath a longhorn-steer mural is prime real estate for kicking back with a few snacks and watching the room — or the televisions.

The separate dining room has high-tops, a cozy lounge area and enough Western bric-a-brac to keep you occupied while you wait for a drink. Dark damask wallpaper gives the room a bordello-meets-Old West-saloon vibe that somehow works.

Bartenders and servers have clearly embraced the assignment, too, going full tilt on Daisy Dukes and boots.

During interviews, Foster said, candidates frequently asked about the dress code.

His answer was essentially: Have fun with it.

They have.

The food

The menu focuses on big flavors and small, shareable plates, with bison sliders, smoked brisket tamales, buffalo chicken dip, jalapeño-pepper egg rolls and ceviche among the early favorites.

The limited all-electric kitchen helped shape the menu, forcing Foster to get creative with just an oven, smoker and a few induction burners.

Dips, ceviches, salads, chili and a small selection of barbecue make for a fun assortment — and some very good bites.

Eventually, Foster envisions a dependable core menu of small plates supplemented by nightly smoker specials, such as tri-tip or ribs.

For now, think smorgasbord rather than four-course meal.

Best bets

Smoked Onion Dip, $13: Just what it says: a big old bowl of onion dip with a hint of smoke and straight-up chips. Add caviar if you’ve just struck oil. It’s pricey but tasty.

Ahi Ceviche Tostada, $20: Solid, simple and fresh, with ruby-red tuna, chipotle aioli, pickled onion and radish. Pepitas and fresh avocado class it up.

Elote Salad, $15: Sweet corn with tangy lime dressing, salty cotija cheese and a few grinds of pepper.

Bison Sliders, $19: One of the best things on the menu. Juicy mini burgers slathered with chimichurri and red-eye glaze. Two-bite brilliance.

Loaded Baked Potato, $19: I’m a sucker for a baked potato. Cover it with cheese béchamel and candied bacon and I’m a goner. Nostalgic and perfect.

Frito Pie, $12: A love-it-or-hate-it proposition. Chili, cheese, tomatoes and Fritos will always have a place in my heart.

More details

For an upcoming Dolly Parton tribute on Sept. 25, Spur will feature musician Max Vogel, along with a Dolly Parton look-alike contest.

Live music is planned about twice a month, with more on the way, along with line dancing, music bingo, karaoke brunch and happy hour.

Spur is family-friendly before 9 p.m., when it becomes 21 and over.

You can show up in boots and a cowboy hat, or just show up. Either way, you’ll probably end up yeehawing at least once.

Open 4-11 p.m. Sunday through Thursday and 4 p.m. to midnight Friday and Saturday. 9000 Windsor Road, Windsor, 707-620-0193, instagram.com/spur.saloon.windsor

title: 90 Kinds of Instant Ramen? Meet Graton Resort’s Wildly Fun New Neon Kitty
summary:
Nearly 90 kinds of instant ramen, Korean hot dogs, onigiri and viral Asian snacks fill the shelves at Graton Resort & Casino’s colorful new Neon Kitty.

The post 90 Kinds of Instant Ramen? Meet Graton Resort’s Wildly Fun New Neon Kitty appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Chef Jennifer Murphy-Ellamar was, understandably, feeling a little thirsty after taste-testing nearly 90 varieties of instant ramen for the shelves of Neon Kitty, the new market and noodlery at Graton Resort & Casino.

Standing before a wall of crinkly plastic packages and cardboard bowls she had handpicked from across Asia, she was searching for a particular favorite: Menraku Tonkotsu, with its creamy pork broth and chewy noodles.

“This is really good,” she said, pulling a package from the shelves she calls her ramen library.

With K-pop humming in the background and a dozen golden maneki-neko waving their lucky paws at us, the choice between creamy tonkotsu and something coated in screaming-hot chiles wasn’t difficult. Screaming-hot chiles never work out in my favor.

So why was a fine-dining chef more accustomed to caviar, lobster and Wagyu tasting menus spending her days with a plastic soup spoon and getting salty tonkotsu broth facials?

Adding “ramen sommelier” to her résumé was simply too irresistible to pass up. And someone had to write the tasting notes for the staff.

All-night noodle party

“A restaurant offering instant ramen is crazy,” Murphy-Ellamar said. “I never thought I’d be doing something like this in my career.”

On opening day, she bustled around what she describes as an “Asian bodega” inside the casino. Flanked by two giant lucky cats, pink neon signs and enough cartoon animals to overcrowd a manga convention, it’s a tween dream wrapped in a fuzzy blanket of kawaii.

Trying to describe Neon Kitty as a cafe, convenience store, bodega or snack bar doesn’t quite do it justice. It’s simply Neon Kitty, and somehow that makes perfect sense.

It is also an oddly obvious solution to a problem at the 13-year-old casino: how to feed guests late at night.

With a hotel, multiple clubs and entertainment venues, in addition to gaming floors, requiring food service around the clock, Murphy-Ellamar turned to one of her favorite foods for something that could be served at any hour — fast, hot and inexpensive, without requiring a full restaurant meal.

Whether it’s 4 p.m. or 4 a.m., the process is simple: Pick a ramen. Any ramen.

Staff members can point out the options — spicy or mild, beef or pork, and everything in between — if you’re stumped. Take the package to the counter and watch as a high-tech machine cooks the noodles at precisely the right temperature. Add fresh toppings like pork, corn, nori and bamboo shoots, and within minutes you’re hunched over a steaming bowl of noodles.

If you’ve experienced the delightfully lowbrow appeal of instant ramen, whether out of economic necessity or pure laziness, the attraction is easy to understand.

“Every culture has their own instant noodle,” Murphy-Ellamar said. “Each one has a different texture. Some are salty and spicy, some are more subtle, and you can really geek out on it.”

The dried-noodle selection includes Vietnamese pho, Thai curries, Chinese seafood broths and dozens of other variations.

But ramen is only part of Neon Kitty.

Viral vibes

Murphy-Ellamar spent months not only handpicking noodles but also creating a lineup of grab-and-go foods made in-house: Japanese egg salad sandwiches, steamed bao and Korean hot dogs, along with social-media darlings like Vietnamese chè thái, a fruit dessert, and Taiwanese fan tuan, a sticky rice breakfast roll.

There are also onigiri, Spam musubi, dumplings, rice bowls, candies, milk tea drinks and shelves of brightly packaged snacks.

The inspiration clearly comes from Japanese convenience stores, known as konbini, which are beloved well beyond Japan for their surprisingly good prepared foods. But Neon Kitty casts a much wider net, drawing from China, Korea, Japan, the Philippines, Vietnam, Thailand and Indonesia.

“It’s not fusion,” Murphy-Ellamar said. “It’s respecting each individual culture.”

Nostalgia or discovery

For a wide swath of Graton’s customers, Neon Kitty offers a familiar taste of home.

The resort draws a significant Asian clientele and regularly hosts Asian performers. A treat that sends one customer into a TikTok-fueled squeal — hint: #chèthái is trending — may be an everyday favorite for someone else.

“A lot of this is nostalgia for me,” Murphy-Ellamar said.

Growing up, the Vietnamese food her mother packed for school sometimes drew teasing from classmates. Decades later, many of those same flavors have become social-media stars.

And that’s exactly the point.

While I’m pondering whether the butter-flavored potato chips are a good idea — yes, yes, they are — someone else might be getting warm fuzzies over a whipped-cream-and-strawberry sandwich reminiscent of a childhood lunch box.

Also a great call.

The changing face of Graton

Neon Kitty is one of several new restaurants reshaping the food lineup at the Rohnert Park casino under Murphy-Ellamar and her husband, chef Roy Ellamar.

Over the past two years, the couple has developed AYA, the resort’s new fine-dining restaurant, along with SoCo Dough Co. and Playbook sports bar. Neon Kitty, in the casino’s new nonsmoking wing, is the latest addition, with more projects still in the works.

But while Neon Kitty is about as far from white-tablecloth dining as you can get, Murphy-Ellamar is clear that it isn’t a throwaway. The same obsessive attention applies here, redirected toward fast-casual craveability and fun.

“It’s impossible to walk by this restaurant and not want to come in,” she said.

And if you decide to taste your way through all 90 ramen varieties, grab a fizzy Ramune soda, milk tea or melon juice.

You’ll need it.

288 Golf Course Drive W., Rohnert Park, 707-588-7100, graton.com/fast-casual/neon-kitty

title: Where to Get the Best Pancakes in Sonoma County
summary:
From fluffy buttermilk to lemon ricotta, here are some of our favorite pancakes in Sonoma County to enjoy on National Pancake Day.

The post Where to Get the Best Pancakes in Sonoma County appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
From ancient Rome to millennial brunch culture, pancakes have long been a breakfast staple — and a natural companion to a mimosa.

Across Sonoma County, chefs put their own spin on the classic stack. Here are some favorites, from fluffy buttermilk pancakes to thin Swedish-style versions and a Dutch Baby big enough to share. Enjoy them on National Pancake Day, Sept. 26, or any day of the year.

Best Newcomer

Dolce Rosa: These plate-size ricotta pancakes are good enough on their own, but the espresso-spiked mascarpone and chocolate syrup, finished with a dusting of cocoa, push them firmly into dessert territory. Breakfast, meet tiramisu. 4910 Sonoma Highway, Suite B, Santa Rosa. 707-931-4625, instagram.com/dolcerosacafe

The Classic

Dierk’s Parkside Café: Simple, fluffy pancakes come with eggs and bacon at this longtime Santa Rosa breakfast favorite. 404 Santa Rosa Ave., Santa Rosa, 707-573-5955, dierksparkside.com

Sweetest Treat

Cafe Carrusel: Strawberry Heaven pink pancakes with sweet glaze and colorful marshmallows are a childhood dream at this pink-on-pink bruncheria in downtown Santa Rosa. The morning-centric menu also includes matcha, ube, blueberry, red velvet, Oreo and classic buttermilk pancakes. 630 Third St., Santa Rosa, 707-655-8365, instagram.com/cafe_carrusel

Sleeper Hit

Fandee’s Restaurant: Rich, fluffy lemon-ricotta pancakes are served with berries and vanilla crème anglaise. 7824 Covert Lane, Sebastopol, 707-829-2462, fandeesrestaurant.com

Best Lemon-Ricotta Hotcake

Acorn Cafe: At the former Oakville Grocery site, Acorn Cafe serves a lemon-ricotta hotcake with house lemon curd, whipped ricotta and oat crumble, topped with lemon-lavender ice cream. 124 Matheson St., Healdsburg, 707-955-7001, acornhealdsburg.com

Big and Buttery

Jeffrey’s Hillside Cafe: Buttermilk pancakes arrive as large as dinner plates, accompanied by two eggs and a choice of bacon, sausage or ham. 2901 Fourth St., Santa Rosa, 707-546-6317, jeffreyshillsidecafe.com

Brunch Favorite

Verano Cafe: Plate-size lemon pancakes get their distinctive texture from cottage cheese, eggs and lemon. Pair them with a mimosa — passion fruit is a favorite — or a cup of coffee. 18976 Sonoma Highway, Sonoma, 707-931-6837, veranocafesonoma.com

Bavarian-Style

Brother’s Cafe: The owners of Sebastopol’s Hole in the Wall opened this sister restaurant in 2022. The standout is the Dutch Baby, a German-style pancake with caramelized sugar and apples. 3135 Cleveland Ave., Santa Rosa, 707-541-6345, brotherscafesr.com

Swedish-Style

Thin, crepe-like pancakes from Sweden aren’t hard to find in Sonoma County.

Baked on the River: The Pancakes from the North are thin and folded, served with vanilla whipped cream, lingonberry jam, butter and maple syrup. 16390 Fourth St., Guerneville, 707-865-6060, bakedontheriver.com

Stockhome: These plate-sized pancakes have crisp edges and a hint of sweetness, and come with vanilla whipped cream and berries. 220 Western Ave., Petaluma, 707-981-8511, stockhomepetaluma.com

Fill ’Er Up

Sax’s Joint: For sheer size, it’s hard to beat the restaurant’s enormous pancake, which is roughly the size of a pizza and made with a half-gallon of batter. 317 Petaluma Blvd. S., Petaluma, 707-559-3021, saxsjoint.com

Farm-to-Table

Americana: Pancakes, hot off the griddle, are top-notch. Choose from classic, blueberry or chocolate-chip pancakes, served with housemade vanilla-cider maple syrup, whipped cream and seasonal fruit. 162 N. Main St., Sebastopol, 707-827-3309; 205 Fifth St., Suite A, Santa Rosa, 707-755-1548, americanasonomacounty.com

Best with Your Dog

Howard Station Cafe: This dog-friendly, locomotive-themed cafe serves stacks of buttermilk, blueberry and banana-walnut pancakes. 3611 Bohemian Highway, Occidental, 707-874-2838, howardstationcafe.com, instagram.com/howardstationcafe

Maci Martell contributed to this article.

title: At Chateau Montelena, Napa Valley’s Past Comes to Life
summary:
A historic Calistoga winery pairs classic wines and a storied estate with an AI-assisted look at the people and places that shaped its past.

The post At Chateau Montelena, Napa Valley’s Past Comes to Life appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
In the last couple of years, Napa Valley has seen a wave of dramatic winery makeovers, from Robert Mondavi Winery’s multimillion-dollar renovation to Beaulieu Vineyard’s recently unveiled refresh. As impressive as those transformations can be, there is something appealing about stepping back in time to the region’s early days.

At Chateau Montelena in Calistoga, classic Napa Valley wines are poured inside a Gothic-style stone castle built in the late 19th century. Now, in a nod to the modern era, visitors can explore the winery’s 144-year history through a storytelling experience that brings historical photographs to life with artificial intelligence.

The story

In 1882, A.L. Tubbs, a San Francisco entrepreneur who had made his fortune during the Gold Rush, bought 254 acres at the foot of Mount St. Helena with plans to build a winery. He planted vineyards on the property, and by 1896, A.L. Tubbs Winery was among Napa Valley’s largest.

The winery closed during Prohibition. Tubbs’s grandson later revived the operation, but it shut down again and the vineyards were sold in 1945.

In 1958, Yort Wing Frank and his wife, Jeanie, bought the property and made the winery their home. To evoke the couple’s homeland in China, Yort created Jade Lake, a water garden with bridges, pagodas and willow trees.

Lee and Helen Paschich acquired the estate and winery a decade later, laying the groundwork for a return to commercial wine production. In 1972, Lee sold the majority of the property to Jim Barrett, a successful business lawyer who dreamed of starting a winery. Barrett replanted the original vineyard with Cabernet Sauvignon.

Four years later, Chateau Montelena’s 1973 Chardonnay made history when it bested its French counterparts in the now-famous 1976 “Judgment of Paris” tasting.

Today, Jim Barrett’s son, Bo, runs the winery. More than 100 acres of the estate are planted to vines, primarily Cabernet Sauvignon, Primitivo and Zinfandel, along with smaller plantings of Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot and Petite Sirah. Last year, the winery added a 72-acre Chardonnay vineyard in Carneros.

The vibe

Before you even reach the ivy-covered winery, the beauty of the estate is hard to miss. From the lower-level parking area, a path leads toward the tasting room through stands of California coast redwoods and a serene water garden, where small islands are linked by bright red bridges. Wine club members can picnic in pagodas on the islands.

Inside, the tasting room has dark wood and exposed stone walls, giving it a distinctly old-world feel. Beyond the entrance bar is a small museum devoted to the winery’s history, followed by another bar and several rooms for private experiences. A front patio welcomes walk-in visitors on weekends.

On the palate

Chateau Montelena’s wines remain true to the restrained style of its early years. Winemaker Matt Crafton makes Chardonnays with a Chablis-like character, while the Cabernet Sauvignons balance power with prominent tannins rather than topple over the top.

The 2023 Napa Valley Chardonnay ($75) is a good reminder of why the variety put the winery on the world wine map. Showing plenty of minerality and acidity, the wine has aromas and flavors of green apples and citrus, and a weighty mouthfeel.

The 2024 Potter Valley Riesling ($45) is a pleasant surprise. Made in an off-dry style, it is floral and bright, with notes of nectarine, Meyer lemon and citrus without seeming overly sweet.

The 2023 Estate Zinfandel ($50), from Calistoga, is the opposite of a jammy fruit bomb. It has a beautiful mixed-berry aroma, with flavors to match, accented by savory, herbaceous notes.

Tastings range from $65 for a selection of current releases to $110 for a vineyard tour and tasting. A private, guided exploration of the vineyards and chateau, including library vintages, costs $300.

Beyond the bottle

If you have seen “Bottle Shock,” the 2008 movie loosely based on the 1976 “Judgment of Paris” tasting, Chateau Montelena’s “Story Behind the Bottle” experience ($75) offers a more grounded way to learn what really happened.

The tasting takes place at an eight-seat bar, where framed historical photographs are animated with artificial intelligence. The effect is a little like the moving portraits in the “Harry Potter” films. A human host provides the narration, telling stories from the winery’s early years while pouring current and library releases.

Chateau Montelena is open from 9:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. daily. 1429 Tubbs Lane, Calistoga. 707-942-5105, montelena.com

Tina Caputo is a wine, food and travel writer whose work has appeared in numerous publications, including SevenFifty Daily, Visit California, HuffPost and Sonoma magazine. Follow Tina on Bluesky @winebroad and view her website at tinacaputo.com.

title: Our Favorite Glamping Spots in Sonoma County
summary:
Become one with nature while enjoying some creature comforts at these luxe glamping spots in Sonoma County.

The post Our Favorite Glamping Spots in Sonoma County appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Sleeping under the stars sounds wonderful until you remember that sleeping on the ground isn’t exactly comfortable and that hot showers are a good thing. In Sonoma County, you can have the best of both worlds — being one with nature while enjoying some creature comforts — at these luxe glamping spots.

Safari West, Santa Rosa

Consistently ranked as one of America’s best glamping spots by USA Today 10Best. Safari through Sonoma’s Serengeti, then spend the night in a luxury tent cabin on the 400-acre wildlife preserve. Overnight stays include a chorus of rare birds as your alarm clock and a continental breakfast. Book a South African-style braai (barbecue) for dinner at the Savannah Café for an additional charge. 3115 Porter Creek Road, Santa Rosa. 800-616-2695, safariwest.com

Sugarloaf Ridge State Park, Kenwood

Four permanent glamping tents are tucked away in the campground at Sugarloaf Ridge State Park in Kenwood. Each canvas tent features a queen bed, futon lounge chairs, rugs, tables, lights, and firewood. Other amenities include a picnic table, fire ring, and outdoor seating, plus 4,900 acres of pristine natural wonder including waterfalls, wildflowers, and majestic redwoods along the miles of hiking and biking trails. The park hosts guided events throughout the year, plus stargazing at the Robert Ferguson observatory. 2605 Adobe Canyon Road, Kenwood. 707-833-5712, sugarloafpark.org

Wildhaven, Healdsburg

Just steps from the Russian River, choose between safari-style canvas tents or cabins equipped with a bed, linens, heated mattress pads, towels, lights, electric outlets and heaters. Each site has a picnic table, fire pit, and access to a communal cooking area with barbecues and sinks. Guests can enjoy easy access to hiking trails, private access to the Russian River for a cooling afternoon dip or float, plus Saturdays bring morning yoga sessions and tasting events with local winemakers. 2411 Alexander Valley Road, Healdsburg. 707-283-7773, wildhavensonoma.com

Lake Sonoma, Geyserville

Camping at Lake Sonoma Recreation Area in Geyserville got an upgrade this summer when The Ranch at Lake Sonoma opened the first of 38 new glamping spots. The luxury canvas tents on wooden platforms are outfitted with full-sized beds and heaters. The second phase of tents will be safari tents from Botswana (which ranch manager Nikki Baxes describes as “showstoppers”) that are expected to be installed by late summer. Guests also have access to hot showers, flushing toilets, barbecues and fire rings, while the Ranch’s barn bar is a short walk away.

Despite the luxury trappings, there’s still plenty of wilderness to be found along the 17,000-acre park’s 50 miles of hiking trails. The highlight of Sonoma County’s newest glamping destination might be the views: sunlight sparkles on the lake by day, and at night, the absence of light pollution makes stargazing spectacular. 100 Lake Sonoma Overlook Road, Geyserville. 707-494-4449, theranchatlakesonoma.com

AutoCamp Russian River, Guerneville

At AutoCamp in Guerneville, guests can choose between staying in a sleek Airstream trailer, luxury tent, or the adorable and budget-friendly Happier Camper, with as much luxury as possible packed into its petite 42 square feet. The clubhouse features spa-style showers and bathrooms, general store, and a complimentary morning granola and coffee bar. On-site bike rentals mean Johnson’s Beach on the Russian River is an easy pedal away. Dog-friendly Airstreams are available for an extra fee. 4120 Old Cazadero Road, Guerneville. 888-405-7553, autocamp.com

River Electric, Guerneville

The Russian River area’s newest resort features 46 furnished tents with hotel-like amenities and access to a central bathhouse. The draw here is the resort’s two sparkling pools: a 60-foot round, family-friendly pool and a smaller adults-only area. The pool bar serves meals until 8 p.m., plus cocktails and snacks until 10 p.m. Stays include a continental breakfast. Although checkout is 11 a.m., guests have until 6 p.m. that day to enjoy the pool and restaurant. The resort also offers day passes to those not staying overnight. 16101 Neeley Road, Guerneville. 707-937-8915, theriverelectric.com

Dawn Ranch, Guerneville

In addition to top-tier dining and luxurious cottages, Dawn Ranch offers nine glamping accommodations near the property’s 120-year-old apple orchard from April to October for those who want a more immersive back-to-nature experience. Queen cabin tents feature private baths, while the king tents have shared bathroom facilities with luxury in mind. At the end of the day enjoy s’mores with guests at the communal campfire or at your accommodation’s private firepit. Borrow one of the resort’s Fender guitars for a sing-along before tucking in for the night. 16467 Highway 116, Guerneville. 707-869-0656, dawnranch.com

Sonoma Zipline Adventures, Occidental

Five treehouses, similar to yurts, form an aerial village in redwood treetops on the Alliance Redwoods property in west county. (There’s also a sixth similar ADA-compliant and accessible ground-level structure.) Every treehouse sleeps up to four, and stays include two zipline tours with Sonoma Zipline Adventures — one on the day you arrive and another before you depart. A gourmet dinner and hot breakfast will also be delivered to your arboreal retreat. 6250 Bohemian Highway, Occidental. 888-494-7868, sonomacanopytours.com

Salmon Creek Ranch, Bodega

Forget the tent. At Salmon Creek Ranch you can stay in a dreamy treehouse complete with heat, electricity and a bathroom. Located on a 400-acre working ranch on the Sonoma Coast, Eagle’s Nest Treehouse is accessed via a 30-foot spiral staircase. It features a queen bed, coffee machine and a wraparound deck for lounging — when you’re not hanging out with the ranch’s resident ducks, cows, goats and livestock guardian dogs. 1400 Bay Hill Road, Bodega. 707-775-9604, salmoncreekranch.com

title: This Spaghetti Squash Recipe Combines the Best of Summer and Fall
summary:
Once you’ve raked a fork through cooked spaghetti squash, there are myriad ways to enjoy the noodles. This recipe is one of our favorites.

The post This Spaghetti Squash Recipe Combines the Best of Summer and Fall appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Not long after pomegranates first appear and we can still find summer produce at our farmers markets, winter squashes reach out to connect late summer with early fall. It is a season of remarkable bounty and deliciousness.

Spaghetti squash, with its sun-like exterior and cooked flesh that shreds into slender noodles, hence its name, is perhaps the best transitional treat. Denser winter squashes require slow and somewhat lengthy cooking, but spaghetti squash can be roasted or steamed relatively quickly and a fork is all you need to extract the noodles. The taste is earthy and slightly sweet, but not as sweet as other winter squashes.

Once you’ve raked a fork through the cooked squash, there are myriad ways to enjoy the noodles, chilled or hot. Thai-inspired salad with spicy dressing makes a refreshing meal on hot days. Make spaghetti squash carbonara, a gluten-free delight without any sacrifice of flavor, or on chilly nights, fry sliced mushrooms and sausages and toss them with the “noodles.” Warm spaghetti squash with five-spice butter makes a delicious bed for roasted chicken.

But in early fall when we still have a colorful cornucopia of cherry tomatoes just begging to be plucked from their stems, combine them with spaghetti squash and tiny shrimp, then toss in a sweet-tart vinaigrette. It makes a dazzling dish to enjoy at home or at a picnic or potluck, as it travels well.

Spaghetti Squash, Cherry Tomatoes and Bay Shrimp with Honey-Pepper Vinaigrette

Serves 4

  • 8 ounces bay shrimp (aka Oregon pink shrimp)
  • 1 small shallot, minced
  • 2 garlic cloves, minced
  • ¾ tsp. kosher salt, plus more to taste
  • 2 tbsp. sherry vinegar
  • 2 tsp. freshly cracked black peppercorns, plus more to taste
  • 2 tbsp. honey, warmed
  • ⅓ to ½ cup extra-virgin olive oil
  • 2 tbsp. shredded fresh spearmint leaves, optional
  • 5 cups (approximately) cooked spaghetti squash, lightly chilled (see note)
  • 1 ½ cups cherry tomatoes, halved if small, quartered if large
  • Spearmint leaves, optional, for garnish

Put the shrimp into a strainer set over a deep bowl or the kitchen sink to drain.

Meanwhile, combine the shallot, garlic and kosher salt in a small bowl, add the vinegar, and set aside for 15 minutes. Stir in the pepper, honey and 1/3 cup of olive oil. Taste and correct for salt, pepper and acid, adding the remaining olive oil if it is too tart. Fold in the mint, if using.

Put the spaghetti squash into a medium bowl, add the cherry tomatoes and half the vinaigrette, and use two forks to toss together gently. Tip into a shallow serving bowl or divide among four individual bowls. Top with the shrimp and spoon the remaining dressing over everything.

Garnish with spearmint leaves, if using, and enjoy right away.

Note: Steaming spaghetti squash instead of roasting in the oven results in the best flavor and light texture ideal for enjoying in these recipes. For about 5 cups, cut a 2 1/2 pound squash in half lengthwise, season lightly with salt, and set both halves, cut side up, in a broad steamer set over a pot of simmering water. Steam until the flesh about half an inch from the peel is just tender when pierced with a fork; do not overcook. Remove it from the heat and let it cool until easy to handle.

Use a grapefruit spoon or a paring knife to remove the seeds and the first thin layer of pulp. Discard it or set seeds aside to roast. Using a dinner fork, work from one end to the other to remove the flesh, which shreds itself as you pull on it. Spread it over a platter or baking sheet to cool completely and then proceed with the recipe.

title: Katie Ambrosi Shares Harvest Season Favorites in Wine Country
summary:
As the new executive director of Wine Road, Katie Ambrosi highlights the joys that have made Wine Country a desired destination for decades.

The post Katie Ambrosi Shares Harvest Season Favorites in Wine Country appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
When Katie Ambrosi took over in June as executive director of Wine Road, an organization that for half a century has helped promote wine tourism in the Russian River, Dry Creek, and Alexander valleys, she stepped into a role that had been held by her predecessor for 25 years during a challenging time for the industry. The Healdsburg native, whose nickname is “Sparkles,” is focused on highlighting the fundamental joys that have made Wine Country a destination for decades.

“Everything’s changed. People are looking at wine in a different way,” she says. “People need to remember that wine tastes good and it’s fun. It’s great with food. It’s something that’s always been a part of celebrations and gatherings and everyday enjoyment. If we can remember that, it goes a long way.”

The mom of two boys — one in college, the other in elementary school — admits to being Healdsburg-centric, but did venture out of the ’burg some when it comes to sharing her favorite things about the harvest season in Sonoma County.

Ambrosi is a keen seamstress and frequently whips up dresses made from thrifted linens, including a gold number she made from a tablecloth for last year’s Sonoma County Harvest Fair celebration. “It showcases so many great things with Sonoma County wine and food all in one spot,” she says of the Harvest Fair. She’s already planning how to bedazzle her dress for the Red, White & Sparkle theme for this year’s Taste, Toast & Celebrate event, on Oct. 10. harvestfair.org

While kids can satisfy their sweet tooth going door-to-door on Halloween, Ambrosi heads to Dry Creek Kitchen for the chocolate peanut butter bar, a grown-up take that puts regular peanut butter cups to shame. “The candy bar dessert is exceptional. You have to make sure you save enough room that you’re able to eat that when you go there.” drycreekkitchen.com

Though not as well known as Geyserville’s famous holiday tractor parade, the town’s annual Fall Colors Festival is a must-do for Ambrosi. “I religiously attend. I have an orange and black full-circle skirt, so I bring my love of vintage dressing to it,” she says, explaining that her costume is tied to the festival’s classic car show. Held on the last Sunday of October, the day also includes a pancake breakfast, a scarecrow display and a pumpkin-decorating contest. visitgeyserville.com/fall-colors

Chances are good you’ll find Ambrosi stepping up to the mic at one of the many local karaoke nights. “I love to sing karaoke, so I have a personal challenge. I want to do one week where we do one song at a different spot every night in Sonoma County.” Two of her favorite haunts are on opposite ends of the county: Railroad Station in Cloverdale and Willowbrook Ale House in Petaluma. railroadstationbarandgrille.com; facebook.com/willowbrook.a.house

50 wineries pouring; local chefs will serve small bites.
